hops.title: Miracle berries make sour taste sweet
hops.text: The small red fruit sold as the miracle berry carries a protein called miraculin that tastes flat on its own. Once it has coated the tongue, though, sour drinks can taste sweet, and the effect can last more than an hour. Ayako Koizumi and colleagues worked out why in cultured cells carrying the human sweet receptor. At neutral pH, miraculin weakened the receptor's response to the sweeteners they tested. When they lowered the pH, miraculin switched the receptor on. So with miraculin present, acid recruits the sweet receptor and adds a sweet signal to a drink that should simply be sour.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A halved yellow lemon glistening with golden droplets beside small glossy red berries on a wooden board.
image.caption: Miraculin lets acid switch on the human sweet receptor, so a sour fruit tastes sweet.

hops.afterHeading: Identity and value can be pulled apart
hops.title: Why you still have room for dessert
hops.text: Next time you are too full for one more bite of dinner yet still want dessert, notice that dinner has not lost its flavor. It still tastes familiar; it has lost its appeal. This is sensory-specific satiety, and Edmund Rolls found it while recording a food-responsive neuron in a monkey's hypothalamus. After the monkey had taken a sweet taste to fullness, the neuron went quiet. Rolls pulled a peanut from his pocket, and at the sight of it the neuron fired hard again. In macaques fed to fullness, taste responses in the insula held steady, while neurons farther downstream in orbitofrontal cortex responded less to the food just eaten.

sources.citation: Rolls, Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience 18(1):nsab044 (2023)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A pushed-aside plate of pasta next to a hand reaching toward a bowl of berry sorbet, with a peanut on a napkin.
image.caption: A food can still taste familiar as it loses its appeal, while a different food still sounds good.

hops.title: Salt-hungry mountain goats and hikers' socks
hops.text: In the 1920s a sportsmen's group released twelve mountain goats into Washington's Olympic Mountains, where the species was not native. The herd grew past a thousand animals and ran into a problem: those mountains have no natural salt licks. Hikers became the salt supply. The goats went after sweat, sweaty socks hung to dry and trailside urine, and some followed people for miles. This is salt seeking in the wild, where even a sweaty sock is worth a goat's attention. Between 2018 and 2020, wildlife crews ran four helicopter capture operations and moved 325 goats, in refrigerated trucks, to their native Cascade Range, where mineral licks exist.

sources.citation: National Park Service, Olympic National Park, Summer 2019 Bugler
National Park Service, Olympic National Park, Mountain Goat Capture and Translocation

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A shaggy white mountain goat on a misty alpine trail sniffing wool hiking socks draped over a wooden post beside a backpack.
image.caption: With no salt licks nearby, Olympic mountain goats treated hikers' sweaty gear as a salt source.
